notes: Brief built normally (135 rules, none parked: no prior instance). Prefill parked 0 rows. Accept-notes: only the dated STATUS line (L10), no carve-out for body wording. Sibling lecture instance apt101-it-runs-overnight already reported the by-morning anchor as a suggestion against this slide; here it is a REVISE because this file owns the body.

resolution.note:
Both refuters killed every blocking finding, so the row stamps PASS:verify-refuted and this REVISE stays as the record. student_facing §22 (No time-of-day anchors in body prose) line 4: scope: I read the rule at its current wording (rule.js student_facing 22). "By morning" is not on its strip list, which names tomorrow, overnight, this morning, tonight, next morning, yesterday and last night. The judge stretched the list by analogy. The rule's own carve-out decides this case: "Mechanics being described (laptop awake, plugged in, walk-away launches) preserved; only time-of-day phrasing changes."

L4 describes the mechanic APT101 teaches. The scheduled digest in curriculum/exercises/apt101-send-it-off.md has "Schedule: daily, early, before Day 2 starts" at L72. Its L7 says the job "runs overnight ... waiting for you when Day 2 starts". "Ready by morning" restates that schedule. It does not assume when the module runs.

The harm the rule prevents is a module whose prose turns false under another cadence. That harm is missing here. The routine runs daily, so with a one-week gap before Day 2 the digest is still "ready by morning".

APT101 is a fixed three-day format built around the overnight digest. The student-facing text says so openly: whats-actually-true.md L5, L9 and L14, our-product-our-system.md L92, the send-it-off phases named "Write the overnight brief", and the routine named "Overnight digest". Every sibling writing judge on those bodies passed §22 for the same reason: the overnight run is the mechanic being taught and the format is fixed. That covers the send-it-off and read-the-digest exercises, all three APT101 module pages, the keep-and-run-tonight exercise, and the slides change-on-recurrence and the-box-is-the-reference. The parent lecture's judge (apt101-it-runs-overnight) also kept this exact line as a suggestion, not a REVISE.

A blocking REVISE on the one phrase gentler than "overnight", in a training whose slide slug, lecture title and exercises all say "overnight", applies the rule inconsistently. It also has no harm behind it. This is at most a suggestion, not a blocking finding. / harm: The judge's facts check out. L4 does carry "ready by morning". "Day 2" appears in L1 and L6. The sibling lecture instance (agentic-product-teams-101--lecture--apt101-it-runs-overnight.writing.json) filed the same line only as a suggestion. §22's word list (overnight / this morning / next morning) does cover "by morning" in spirit.

The harm claim is where the finding fails. Under lenses (a), (b) and (d) it doesn't hold for APT101:

1. **The rule's premise does not fit this training.** §22 rests on "Single module can run any time of day with any gap to next", which is the AE101 module-on-customer-cadence model. APT101 is a three-day training, and the overnight run is built into its mechanics, not just its wording:
   - Day 1 module (our-product-our-system.md L92): "Your laptop, with the overnight digest scheduled, plugged in, lid open. Day 2 opens on what came back."
   - The agent's own path is `module-2/morning-agent/morning.md` (L129-131).
   - Day 2's handoff ID is `apt101-d2-what-ran-overnight`.
   
   "Ready by morning" describes how the training actually works. Nobody in the room would be misled or worse off.

2. **Another line already carries the meaning, so the fix changes nothing (lens d).** Student-facing APT101 body prose says "overnight" in several places:
   - whats-actually-true.md L5: "Agents keep working between sessions and overnight"
   - whats-actually-true.md L9: "an agent that ran overnight"
   - whats-actually-true.md L14: "Check an overnight digest"
   - our-product-our-system.md L92: "the overnight digest scheduled"
   
   Removing two words from this one slide leaves the training exactly as tied to an overnight gap as before. If the cadence lock is a real defect, it lives in the training's design and its module bodies, not in this slide.

3. **The harm restates the rule (lens b).** "fixes a time of day in the body" just says the rule was tripped. It names no concrete failure. Even if Day 2 came a week later, "ready by morning" would still be true. It is not a false statement.

4. **The fix has a cost.** It rewrites a backing claim quote (`digest-overnight`) whose stated design rationale is "the overnight digest is Day 1's send-off". That is churn against a deliberate design, applied to a simulation training whose maintainer reads every page when the flag comes off.

Net: the finding is technically a rule hit, but in this training it is tidiness, and the fix moves no reader. Refuted.
